title: Create a trading system
summary: Define its name, description, tags, entry checklist, risk rules, and exit rules.
outcome: You will build a complete trading system with entry, risk, exit, and no-trade rules.
before: Write down the market, timeframe, and trade direction addressed by the system.
Prepare at least one entry condition that can be judged objectively.
Distinguish a discretionary trading system from an automated backtest strategy; they serve different purposes.

sections.title: 1. Add a name, description, and tags
sections.body: Go to Strategy → Systems and create a trading system. Use a name that distinguishes the market and version, describe when it applies, and add tags for filtering trades later.

sections.title: 2. Write the entry rules
sections.body: Break conditions into rule groups that can be judged, and mark them as automatic, semi-automatic, or manual. Avoid descriptions such as “feels good” or “nice pattern” that cannot be verified later.

sections.title: 3. Complete risk and exit rules
sections.body: The risk module should cover at least risk per trade, stop location, and scaling rules. The exit module should define profit-taking, trailing protection, time-based exits, or signal invalidation.

sections.title: 4. Add no-trade rules
sections.body: Record situations that require you to stand aside, such as before scheduled data, after consecutive losses, during abnormal spreads, or without a stop. No-trade rules often reduce impulsive decisions more effectively than adding more entry conditions.

sections.title: 5. Use the system in practice
sections.body: After saving, select the system and complete its checklist before placing an order. When the trade ends, record execution and deviations in History or the strategy journal.

callout.title: A system checklist records compliance by default
callout.body: To block orders when conditions are missing, enable an enforced gate in order discipline as well.

success: The system includes entry, risk, exit, and no-trade modules.
Every main rule can clearly pass or fail.
Practice trades can be linked to the system.

faq.q: What is the difference between a trading system and a backtest strategy?
faq.a: A trading system manages the complete discretionary decision and discipline process. A backtest strategy is an expression that historical data can execute. They can validate each other, but they are not the same object.
No. Keep only conditions you can explain, execute, and review. Too many rules make hindsight selection easier.

faq.q: Will changing a system affect old trades?
faq.a: Old trades should retain the execution record from that time. Create a new version for major changes so that the results can be compared.
